summary: Explains why signaling compression is needed in cellular systems such as GSM and UMTS, where radio capacity is precious and SIP and SDP messages are large. It lists requirements and assumptions for a compression scheme used for this purpose.

plainLanguage.summary: Sending words over radio costs money and time. This document explains why shrinking call-setup messages helps phones, and what a good shrinking method must do.

questions: how does compression help cellular networks
what protocols are targets for sigcomp
subtitle: Requirements for compressing signaling protocol messages in wireless networks.

tldr.problem: Signaling protocols like SIP and RTSP are text-based and verbose, making them expensive to transmit over bandwidth-limited cellular radio links. A typical SIP call setup requires kilobytes of messages over a 9600-bit link, causing delays of several seconds.
tldr.mechanism: This document specifies the requirements and assumptions that a compression scheme must meet to efficiently compress arbitrary signaling protocol messages, particularly for cellular systems like GSM and UMTS, while maintaining transparency and working with existing protocols.
tldr.outcome: The requirements led to the development of the SigComp protocol (RFC 3320 and 3321), which provides stateful compression of signaling messages suitable for wireless networks.

today: RFC 3322 specifies requirements for signaling compression. The resulting SigComp protocol was defined in RFC 3320 (Signaling Compression) and RFC 3321 (Signaling Compression Protocol). Both remain Internet Standards.

sections.title: Why Signaling Compression Matters
sections.content:
In wireless cellular systems like GSM and UMTS, radio spectrum is limited and expensive. Each user must be allocated a small slice of bandwidth. When application-layer signaling protocols such as SIP and RTSP are used in these systems, the messages themselves consume significant radio capacity.

While header compression for IP, UDP, and RTP has been studied, the signaling protocol messages themselves are often larger. These messages are text-based and include redundant information. Compressing them can reduce setup delays and improve call quality, especially for services like Internet telephony where perceived latency directly affects user experience.
sections.plainLanguage: Sending words over a phone's radio connection costs time and money. Shrinking the setup messages means faster calls and better service.

sections.title: The Call Setup Delay Problem
sections.content:
A typical SIP/SDP call setup involves six to eight messages totaling 3,000 to 4,000 bytes. Over a 9,600-bit cellular link with a 140-millisecond round-trip time, this creates a total call setup delay of over four seconds. When combined with other signaling (RSVP, session management), the total delay can exceed six to eight seconds. In contrast, traditional GSM circuit-switched call setup takes only about 3.6 seconds.

This delay is caused not just by radio transmission time but by protocol round trips where the sender must wait for a response before sending the next message. Compression directly addresses the transmission time portion of this problem.
sections.plainLanguage: With uncompressed messages, a phone call setup can take twice as long as it should. Compression cuts the delay.

sections.title: Protocol Characteristics and Alternatives
sections.content:
SIP, RTSP, and SDP are all ASCII-based protocols with similar characteristics: they use a request-response pattern where the sender waits for a reply, messages tend to be verbose to provide necessary information, and many header fields are repeated across messages. The similarities suggest a single generic compression scheme could efficiently handle all of them.

Alternative solutions to the problem exist: increasing bandwidth per user (economically infeasible), decreasing round-trip latency (requires system changes), changing protocol sequences (violates end-to-end transparency), or stripping fields (loses necessary information). Compression is the most practical approach as it maintains transparency and works with existing protocols without modification.
sections.plainLanguage: Lots of different signaling protocols have the same problem: they are too verbose for slow radio links. One compression method can handle them all.

sections.title: General and Performance Requirements
sections.content:
The compression scheme must preserve transparency: when a message is compressed and decompressed, it must be bitwise identical to the original. This ensures no protocol semantics are lost. It must work with both reliable transport (TCP) and unreliable transport (UDP), must be compatible with header compression, must not require modifications to the protocols being compressed, and must work for arbitrary message streams without making assumptions about message patterns.

Performance-wise, the scheme must scale to devices with varying processor and memory capabilities, must not noticeably add to user-perceived delay, must handle message loss and modest reordering (1-2 messages) without preventing decompression of later messages, and must be resilient against undetected errors from lower layers.
sections.plainLanguage: The compression must be perfect—no information can be lost. It must work for any message stream, handle slow devices, and keep working even if some messages are lost.

sections.title: Robustness and Error Handling
sections.content:
Cellular radio links are inherently unreliable. Before error correction, bit error rates can be around 10%; even with forward error correction and interleaving, rates of 10e-3 with variations of 10e-2 to 10e-4 are common. The compression scheme must be resilient against residual errors undetected by lower layers.

Critically, if a compressed message is damaged or lost, it must not prevent decompression of later messages. This is called error propagation minimization. If one message fails to decompress, the next message should still be decodable. Additionally, the scheme should allow correct decompression of messages that arrive slightly out of order.
sections.plainLanguage: Radio links sometimes lose data or get errors. Compression can't stop working if one message is bad—the next messages must still decompress.
